summary: Mars Atlas answers the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge with a layered, integrated map that helps a human explorer plan and carry out a Marswalk. It combines data from several NASA missions (Viking, Mars Global Surveyor MOLA, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE and CTX, and Mars Express HRSC) in one free browser app that takes you from NASA's 3D model of the whole planet down to 25 cm HiRISE imagery of Jezero Crater, where you can draw a traverse, see its distance, slope and climb on a real 20 m USGS CTX height model, and compare alternative routes. What makes it different is honesty: every number says what it rests on (measured, calculated, illustrative or your own note), slopes outside the data are "unknown", never "flat", and the app explains why one route beats another and at what trade-off that stops being true. It also helps plan the science along the way: observations, sample sites and science targets are pinned to the route, and the safety step shows the point of no return, oxygen and power needs, and the Earth-Mars message delay. It matters because mission planning, teaching and public outreach all need tools that turn open NASA data into decisions people can understand and check, without installing anything.
details:
What it does

Mars Atlas lets anyone plan and analyze a surface traverse on Mars in a web browser.

  • Whole planet to ground. A 3D Mars built on NASA/JPL's 3D model and lifted by MOLA heights, with four surface maps, 29 real places (rover and lander sites, volcanoes, canyons) with NASA photos, and routes that follow the surface anywhere with distances on Mars's real radius. A 2D map uses NASA Mars Trek tiles: Viking colour, MOLA relief, CTX and HiRISE (25 cm) around Jezero.
  • Plan. Draw routes, move and reorder waypoints, add georeferenced observations with notes and photos, mark exclusion zones, undo and redo.
  • Analyze, in eight explained steps. Size, height, legs, comparison, 3D fly-over with a synchronized height profile, decision checklist, questions and safety. Each step has a chart and a plain sentence built from the route's own numbers.
  • Why this route? One slider sets the penalty λ in the route cost C = D + λ(A + H) (distance against total ascent and descent). A table re-ranks the candidate routes live and names the exact penalty at which the winner changes.
  • Planning Lab. 25 small, explained "what if" models: why there is no route (it relaxes one constraint at a time and names the blocker), whether the preferred route stays preferred under terrain uncertainty, radio relay sites from line of sight on real heights, battery and temperature over a sol, and more.
  • Safety step. Point of no return where the reserve no longer covers a retrace, a kit computed from the route's oxygen and power, and the 3 to 22 minute Earth-Mars message delay.
  • Teams. Optional accounts save missions to the cloud and share them with teammates as viewer or editor, protected by database row-level security. Guests can use everything without an account.

How it works

The app is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript ES modules with Three.js for 3D, with no build step. Map tiles stream from NASA's Mars Trek WMTS services in an equirectangular projection. Terrain numbers come from a clip of the USGS Mars 2020 Terrain Relative Navigation CTX DTM (20 m posts) bundled with the app. Routing uses A* on the height grid with a slope limit and slope cost, D* Lite for fast replanning after a change, and a bounded multi-objective search that returns the Pareto set of routes (no route in the set is both shorter and flatter than another). Optional cloud saving uses Supabase with row-level security.

Why it can be trusted

  • Every number carries a label: measured (NASA/USGS), calculated, illustrative scenario, or user note.
  • A reproducible benchmark: three routes on the Jezero delta, stored as fixed coordinates, are re-planned by the test suite on every change, which fails if a number drifts.
  • The formulas in the README (distance, slope, route cost, oxygen and energy) are worked examples checked by automated tests.
  • Over 260 automated tests plus browser tests in GitHub Actions that load real NASA tiles, check zoom, pan, slow network, offline recovery and phone layouts.
  • We state clearly what it is not: not a navigation tool, not a safety approval, not endorsed by NASA. The resource and Lab models are illustrative.

Benefits

  • Students and teachers get an interactive way to understand Mars geography, scale and the trade-offs of exploration.
  • Mission-planning enthusiasts and researchers get fast, repeatable first-order route analysis on real NASA data.
  • The public sees how open NASA data becomes a decision, and where the data stops.

What we hope to achieve

A classroom-ready tool for planetary science, and a foundation for sharper terrain (more height models, other landing sites), terrain-aware speed and power models, and real-time collaboration.

Tools and languages

JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, Three.js, Python (data preparation of the DTM clip), Node.js test runner, Playwright (browser tests), GitHub Actions, Vercel (hosting), Supabase (optional accounts and cloud saving).
dataRefs: Mars 2020 TRN CTX DTM Mosaic (Fergason et al. 2020)
